p_value.name: p-value
p_value.correct: The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
p_value.misconception: The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true (so 1 - p is the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true).

significance_vs_effect.name: statistical significance vs. effect size
significance_vs_effect.correct: Statistical significance says little about the size or practical importance of an effect; with large samples, tiny effects become significant.
significance_vs_effect.misconception: A statistically significant result means the effect is large or practically important.

nonsignificance.name: non-significant results
nonsignificance.correct: A non-significant result means the data do not provide enough evidence for an effect; it does not show that there is no effect, especially in small samples.
nonsignificance.misconception: A non-significant result proves that there is no effect (or that two conditions are equally good).

confidence_interval.name: confidence interval
confidence_interval.correct: A 95% confidence interval is a range of plausible values for a population parameter (e.g. the mean); it does not describe where individual observations lie.
confidence_interval.misconception: A 95% confidence interval contains about 95% of the individual observations (it describes the range of the data).

correlation_causation.name: correlation vs. causation
correlation_causation.correct: A correlation in observational data does not show that one variable causes the other; confounders or reverse causation may explain it.
correlation_causation.misconception: A correlation between two variables shows that one causes the other.

standard_error.name: standard error vs. standard deviation
standard_error.correct: The standard error describes the uncertainty of the mean (SE = SD / sqrt(n)); the spread of individual observations is the standard deviation.
standard_error.misconception: The standard error describes how much individual observations vary around the mean.
